chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
title: Stock cards, theater bookings and how the lawyer ruined it
summary: The tour did percentage in theaters until his West Indian lawyer took deposit money, so he dropped the show and Little Richard moved on.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: This was the sort of time when packages were the thing.

Yeah, could do it. Everybody was wondering -- Pasadena printed on the cards and he said Gail called him, Evans come down. Everybody wanted to know who's backing the show. Who's got this show out? Because the stock cards was beautiful. I had a group called the Durmettes, organized a group of girls and had them singing. Well, they

were in the band, too, but they had time to go back and change costumes, different outfit. So it was a big show. It was doing percentage, guaranteed percentage in the theaters. 50 percent houses. It was getting that crowd. They was going after those girls like everything.

So, that's one of the periods in there. I stayed out there about seven weeks, something like that. Didn't do no one-nighters. All theaters. ________ let the band go. I mean, I was supposed to have went to California with the show. The contact really come through ________, the guy who got all the theaters?
(Inaudible) book me a hundred theaters through because he didn't have those middlemen, you understand?

And in my management, started to mess it up because I had a lawyer in New York, a West Indian lawyer, and he started fooling with the deposits when they come in. He took $2,000 of the money and went out and bought him -- put it down and bought him a home with that.

We got ready for the money and that money wasn't there and he just kept on doing things, and I dropped the whole thing. I said wrong set-ups beind me, got to close it. I brought everybody back. Little Richard went on. Short while,
his record come out. He already recorded.
